ety.text: From Middle English vomiten, from Latin vomitāre (“vomit repeatedly”), frequentative form of vomō (“be sick, vomit”), from Proto-Indo-European *wemh₁- (“to spew, vomit”). Cognate with Old Norse váma (“nausea, malaise”), Old English wemman (“to defile”). More at wem.

senses.d: To regurgitate or eject the contents of the stomach through the mouth; puke.
ex: The fish […] vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.

senses.d: To regurgitate and discharge (something swallowed); to spew.
To eject from any hollow place; to belch forth; to emit.
ex: She snapped and started vomiting curses at us.
Like the sons of Vulcan, vomit smoke.

senses.d: The regurgitated former contents of a stomach; vomitus.
ex: For all tables are full of vomite and filthinesse, so that there is no place cleane.

senses.d: Anything that is worthless; rubbish; trash.
ex: "[Y]ou've spent so much of your life writing romantic vomit for morons that the mushy bit of the brain you did have has gone rancid."

senses.d: That which causes vomiting; an emetic.
ex: He gives your Hollander a vomit.
